episode_thesis: Simon Judes, co-CIO of Winton (Top Traders Unplugged 139, uploaded 21 March 2023), argues that Winton's edge comes from empirical scientific research with strict data-mining controls, rejecting the efficient market hypothesis, and from hyper-vigilant risk management that goes beyond volatility. Long-term trend following Sharpe is about 0.5 (declining as the number of traders grew, with fast trend deteriorating most), so Winton runs a diversified CTA that is 75% trend and 25% other signals, adds genuinely diversifying alternative markets (effective number of markets, not raw count), lets humans own key parameters, refuses to switch trend speed on regime (that is an implicit call on the Fed), and sees trend as often contrarian to prevailing narratives. Kaastrup-Larsen pushes the portfolio-Sharpe framing and challenges the 'more markets' claim; Dunne adds that falling costs and fees partly offset the lower gross Sharpe.

speakers.name: Simon Judes
speakers.role: Guest; co-CIO of Winton (joined July 2008; firm founded about 25 years earlier by David Harding, about 200 staff, USD 10bn AUM)
speakers.speaker_note: Speaks for Winton as a firm. Statements about David Harding's 2018 comments are relayed. The 2023 market-position remarks (short bonds, long equities) describe Winton's trend book at the time of recording (about March 2023). The replication fee figure (about 95bp) is the host's, not his (ledger correction applied).

worldview_premises.premise: The efficient market hypothesis is not the right foundation: with hard work and scientific analysis good predictions about markets are possible, so one approaches markets with an open mind rather than preconceived theories.
worldview_premises.support: Winton's founding experience; David Harding found EMH to be a headwind for years.

worldview_premises.premise: Early market experiences (1987, 2008) shape how researchers and firms parametrise and organise trend strategies, a behavioural source of differences between trend followers.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience of joining in July 2008 and Harding's 1987 experience; observation of firms that started after 2008.

worldview_premises.premise: Data-mining false positives are the central threat to research; they are avoided by shared statistical techniques for multiple and sequential hypothesis testing and by a process that stops researchers privately overfitting many ideas and presenting only the good subset.
worldview_premises.support: Describes hiring, training and process; no specific tests or thresholds quoted.

worldview_premises.premise: Confidence in a new signal comes from backtest statistics (Sharpe, correlation to existing strategies) plus, when available, an economic rationale with testable intermediate relationships; lack of rationale lowers confidence but does not kill the idea. The sources of alpha are a mixture of behavioural, structural and microstructure effects, so who is on the other side is hard to say.
worldview_premises.support: Winton practice.

worldview_premises.premise: Long-term trend following Sharpe is about 0.5, which is scarcely enough on its own to run a fund; other signals should be added to raise Sharpe. Trend performance has declined steadily since the 1970s (first seen in Winton research around 2007), not only after 2008.
worldview_premises.support: Harding's 2018 statement and Winton long-horizon research on the strategies in use at the time.

worldview_premises.premise: The decline correlates strongly with growth in the number of traders of the strategy, so 0.5 is the expectation; long simulations show only that underlying markets trend, not what a crowded real strategy will earn.
worldview_premises.support: Observed correlation over the last 50 years with industry growth; no figures given.

worldview_premises.premise: Fast trend strategies deteriorated most since 1997 because everyone traded them; slow strategies started with lower Sharpe. Pure Sharpe maximisation favours very slow trend, but investors also want responsiveness at turning points like 2008 and 2022.
worldview_premises.support: Winton analysis of speeds (paper on its website).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend cannot be timed and a good year does not predict a bad next year (good years come in sequences), but allocators bear personal risk if trend underperforms right after they allocate, so their concerns should be addressed (for example averaging in over months) rather than answered with statistics.
worldview_premises.support: Winton's pre-2008 record of good years; allocator conversations.

worldview_premises.premise: Allocators drop trend after long drawdowns not for lack of faith but because each line item must be justified to an investment committee; smoothing drawdowns has great value but adding non-trend signals necessarily reduces crisis effectiveness, so the type and weight of added signals matter.
worldview_premises.support: Allocator experience and Winton's own trade-off.

worldview_premises.premise: Liquidity, opportunism and no bias are necessary but not sufficient for crisis performance; trend works in extended trends and fails when equities rise steadily then reverse sharply (February 2018). Labels like 'crisis alpha' mislead, so describe the response in different environments instead.
worldview_premises.support: Historical record of trend in crises, February 2018 as counterexample.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is often contrarian to prevailing fundamental narratives (oil in 2014 when shale supply was underestimated against a peak-oil view; German yields falling into negative territory against the belief they could never go below zero), and trends extend in time precisely when a narrative says the market must go the other way.
worldview_premises.support: Two named examples.

worldview_premises.premise: Slow-horizon strategies have too few independent events for machine learning (one cannot rerun a crash; observational science), while fast intraday strategies have many observations and suit machine learning (experimental science).
worldview_premises.support: Winton paper on observational versus experimental science; astronomy versus particle-physics analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: Sharpe scales with the square root of the effective number of markets, not the count: 50-60 classical markets may be only 8-10 independent, so adding genuinely different markets adds a lot. Alternative markets outperformed major markets over the last decade, including the post-crisis period when mainstream trend struggled.
worldview_premises.support: Correlation arithmetic; European gas up tenfold as the largest trend he has seen; no performance table quoted.

worldview_premises.premise: Alternative markets earn extra return partly because barriers to entry (software, operations, middle office) keep trend followers from extending into them; many OTC alternatives can be cleared on exchange, reducing counterparty risk toward major-futures levels.
worldview_premises.support: Winton's own build-out experience.

worldview_premises.premise: Risk is not volatility: volatility is easy to estimate but loss risk is hard (VIX at record lows in 2017 while valuations were rich), so use many risk measures and scenarios.
worldview_premises.support: The 2017 low-VIX / rich-valuation example.

worldview_premises.premise: Claiming that a systematic process is fully automated hides that someone must still choose the parameters or the algorithm that picks them (an infinite regress); a firm must decide at which level humans take responsibility, and Winton pushes responsibility to humans fairly early (trend speed, asset allocation).
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from first principles; not a result.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why switching trend speed with the regime is an implicit Fed call

steps.from: February-March 2020: markets fall for a month until the Fed intervenes
steps.to: Fast trend beats slow trend (turn positions short within two weeks and profit as the fall continues; slow trend loses on the way down and again on the rebound)
steps.why: Short duration of the fall before policy intervention.

steps.from: Two weeks into the fall with a slow trend long
steps.to: Choosing to speed up is right only if the Fed steps in later, wrong if it steps in now, and about the same if it does not step in
steps.why: The decision amounts to a bet on what the Fed will do and when.

steps.from: No evidence that fast trend's edge persisted
steps.to: Slower trend did better again afterwards; no regime-based speed switching
steps.why: Predicting policy is the job of discretionary macro managers, not systematic managers.

mechanism_chains.evidence: The 2020 episode and subsequent performance; qualitative scenario reasoning.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; a systematic speed switch that does not rely on policy forecasts is not considered.

mechanism_chains.topic: Adding non-trend signals: smoothing versus convexity

steps.from: Long drawdowns in trend between 2008 and 2022
steps.to: Allocators drop trend because each line item must be justified

steps.from: Add non-trend signals (carry, statistical, economic, faster technical)
steps.to: Smoother drawdowns but less crisis effectiveness
steps.why: Trade-off in type and weight; carry in equities would add long equity bias and reduce convexity, so carry is traded in commodities and fixed income as well as currencies, where small-gain/large-loss is mitigated.

steps.from: Winton sets 75% trend / 25% other and fixes it
steps.to: Trend profile retained with some drift, and investors know what they receive
steps.why: Mix depends on opportunity set but is fixed deliberately.

steps.to: Split into pure trend, diversified CTA and multi-strategy products
steps.why: Offer choice rather than abandon trend.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Winton's product design and the 2008/2022 record.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If added signals are mostly slow and economically related they reduce convexity in crises.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why more genuinely different markets add return

steps.why: Equity indices, bond futures and many commodities are highly correlated.

steps.from: Add Chinese futures, regional gas, power, freight, marine fuel (not equity sector ETFs or developed-market swaps)
steps.to: Large diversification and large trends (gas up tenfold)
steps.why: Genuinely alternative and additive; barriers to entry keep others out.

steps.from: Access via onshore, internationalised contracts, swaps and QFI; clearing on exchange where possible
steps.why: Operations and software built to absorb markets without large headcount growth.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Correlation arithmetic and recent trends; no portfolio-level performance numbers given.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: When added markets are correlated with vanilla ones or are easy for competitors to access.

mechanism_chains.topic: Scenario-based risk management and the 2013 taper tantrum

steps.from: Replay current positions through every historical environment (worst day/week), e.g. the 1990 Gulf War oil jump of 30%
steps.to: Ask whether that loss is acceptable
steps.why: By definition anything that happened is realistic.

steps.from: Before 2013 trend was long bonds and long stocks with negative correlation; scenario in which correlation turns positive
steps.to: Loss judged unacceptable, volatility run lower

steps.from: March 2023: short bonds, long equities, modestly positive stock-bond correlation because of the inflation dynamic
steps.to: Main worry is a classic risk-off (bonds rally, equities fall) on disinflationary bad news; leverage may be held in a band
steps.why: That scenario is worst for the current book.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Judes concedes the worst case imaginable is everything to zero, so scenarios must be anchored in realism.

decision_process.practice: Two research streams: finding new alpha sources (ideas or data), and maintaining existing ones (reviewing trend speed, signal construction and volatility models); do original research rather than rely on academic journals, including ideas found in Chinese commodity markets that work globally.
decision_process.why: Journals are not at the forefront of alpha research; large research department.

decision_process.practice: Test many hypotheses with simultaneous and sequential multiple-testing techniques and a process that exposes all attempted ideas, not just the best backtests; hire and train for statistical competence.

Update models after market events (February 2007 reversal that hit CTA positions led to volatility-model changes that helped in February 2018) but do not conclude a regime has changed from one episode (March 2020).
decision_process.why: Learning from new event types without overreacting to single occurrences.

decision_process.practice: Keep trend as the core (about 75% of the diversified CTA), add carry (not in equities), statistical, economic and faster technical signals; add new signals each year.
decision_process.why: Raise Sharpe while preserving the trend profile.

decision_process.practice: Parameters mostly universal across markets, adjusted for transaction costs, market impact, spreads and commissions; trend speed chosen with some faster component for turning points even at lower Sharpe; no regime-based speed switching.
decision_process.why: Investor objectives and implicit policy call.

decision_process.practice: Prioritise effective number of markets: add Chinese futures, regional gas and power, freight, marine fuel; avoid equity sector ETFs and developed-market swaps correlated with existing exposure.

Access Chinese futures onshore, through internationalised contracts, via swaps and via the QFI route; clear OTC alternative markets on exchange where possible; invest in software and automation to absorb markets.
decision_process.why: Reduce counterparty risk and operating burden.

decision_process.practice: Replay current positions through all historical environments, run stylised correlation-flip stress tests, look beyond volatility, and let leverage float with signal strength and correlation inside a band decided by the risk measures.
decision_process.why: Risk is not volatility; correlation flip tested in 2013.

decision_process.practice: Fix the trend/non-trend mix; offer pure trend, diversified and multi-strategy products and bespoke programs (varying alternative-market or China exposure more than trend share); offer capped-equity-long trend as an option.
decision_process.why: Allocator drawdown tolerance and process vary; cap lowers long-term performance in proportion but helps the crisis profile.

decision_process.practice: Humans own early design decisions (trend speed, asset allocation, overall strategy leverage, adding a signal) made with analysis; optimisers are used where they do not obscure understanding of the portfolio.
decision_process.why: Preserve understanding and responsibility; machine learning reserved for fast intraday strategies.

decision_process.practice: Single-manager risk is mitigated by fund of funds (with lost fee netting), not by regression-based replication, which is itself a single manager.
decision_process.why: Replication is another manager; using several trend managers trades fee netting for diversification.

speakers.evidence_style: Scientific-method framing with emphasis on statistical controls against data-mining; historical event studies (1987, 2007, 2008, 2013, 2014, 2018, 2020, 2022); correlation arithmetic; scenario replays; few numerical results quoted.

current_views.view: No reason to think 2023 will be bad because 2022 was good; averaging in over several months is a reasonable way to address timing concerns.
current_views.reasoning: Good years come in sequences; 2008 followed good years.

current_views.view: Expected long-term trend Sharpe is about 0.5 and slower trend has done better again since 2020, so no change in the view that trend remains Winton's biggest source of return.
current_views.reasoning: Industry growth correlates with decline; no evidence that faster trend's 2020 outperformance persisted.

current_views.view: Current trend positions are short bonds and long equities, so the key scenario risk is a disinflationary risk-off with bonds rallying and equities falling; stock-bond correlation is modestly positive because of inflation.
current_views.reasoning: Positioning of the book and recent correlation.

current_views.view: Alternative markets have outperformed major markets over the last decade (2022 was the first year not substantially true); European gas and power produced huge trends.
current_views.reasoning: Low correlation and barriers to entry.

current_views.view: Winton's 2023 priorities are original research for new alpha sources and improving existing ones, and hyper-vigilant risk management monitoring many scenarios.
current_views.reasoning: What matters is what can be controlled.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.speaker_note: Most turns are questions, but he states views on Sharpe framing, investors' timing mindset and number of markets. His own firm offers a major-markets trend strategy (a conflict of interest in the 'more markets' debate).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following should be judged by the improvement in total-portfolio Sharpe it delivers, not by its stand-alone Sharpe or a 'crisis alpha' mandate, because Sharpe was not created for single-strategy evaluation.
worldview_premises.support: Reaction to the AQR paper on trend mandates.

worldview_premises.premise: Crisis alpha originally meant three traits (liquid, opportunistic, unbiased long or short), as Kaminski explains: in 2020 the best trade was long bonds and short energy, in 2022 the opposite.
worldview_premises.support: Katie Kaminski interview on the same podcast.

worldview_premises.premise: Potential investors treat trend following as a tactical trade and assume that after a strong 2022 it is too late or cannot repeat, a market-timing mindset that trend followers need to counter.
worldview_premises.support: Investor conversations while travelling.

worldview_premises.premise: A 50-60 market classical portfolio already includes diversified commodities, and going from 100 to 200 markets mostly adds correlated financial markets unless the extras are genuinely alternative (such as Chinese futures); he sees no huge long-term performance difference between managers with different market counts.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of manager track records; no data quoted.

steps.to: Potential investors assume it is too late or cannot repeat
steps.why: Treat trend as a trade to be timed.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Judes replies that good years come in sequences.

decision_process.practice: Frames the discussion around portfolio Sharpe improvement rather than stand-alone Sharpe or labels.

speakers.evidence_style: Anecdote, industry conversations and published papers (AQR, Kaminski).

current_views.view: The investor mindset after 2022 that it is too late for trend is wrong and needs to be countered.
current_views.reasoning: Market-timing notion applied to a strategy that adapts.

current_views.view: Going from 100 to 200 markets mostly adds correlated financial markets unless genuinely alternative.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.speaker_note: Mostly asks questions; one stated view, mapped for completeness.

worldview_premises.premise: Lower trading costs and lower fees partly offset the decline in gross trend Sharpe, so the investor's net outlook is less negative than the 0.5 gross estimate suggests.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from cost and fee trends; no numbers.

speakers.evidence_style: Asks structured questions drawn from other guests' research (100-200 year trend studies).

current_views.view: Net-of-cost trend outlook is better than the gross 0.5 Sharpe suggests because costs and fees have fallen.

disagreements.topic: Does trading more (alternative) markets improve long-term performance?

positions.speaker: Simon Judes
positions.position: Yes: only 8-10 of 50-60 markets are independent, alternative markets outperformed major markets over the decade, and the markets added must be genuinely alternative.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Sees no huge difference in long-term performance between managers; 50-60 classical markets already diversified; going from 100 to 200 mostly adds correlated financial markets. Judes largely agrees on that last point.

positions.speaker: Simon Judes
positions.position: Expectation is about 0.5 gross, because performance declines as more traders do the strategy; long simulations show only that markets trend.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Lower trading costs and fees partly offset the lower gross Sharpe for investors.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Judge trend by improvement in portfolio Sharpe, not stand-alone Sharpe.

disagreements.topic: Is trend following a herding strategy?

positions.speaker: Simon Judes
positions.position: No: it is often contrarian to the prevailing narrative (oil 2014, German yields into negative territory).

positions.speaker: Critics (as characterised by Judes, not speakers)
positions.position: A dumb strategy of people following each other in herd behaviour.

disagreements.topic: Can regression-based CTA replication mitigate single-manager risk?

positions.speaker: Simon Judes
positions.position: No: the replicator is itself a single manager; a fund of funds is the way to diversify manager risk, with its own pros and cons.

positions.speaker: Replication providers (as characterised by Judes, not speakers)
positions.position: Claim that replication mitigates single-manager risk.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The argument that switching speed is an implicit Fed call applies equally to choosing any fixed speed, and Winton does choose a mix of speeds partly for turning points (2008, 2022); the distinction between a static and a dynamic choice is asserted rather than argued.

The claim that trend decline correlates strongly with growth in the number of traders is stated without data or measure of trader count; alternative explanations (market structure, costs) are not discussed.
No Sharpe, return or drawdown numbers are given for Winton products, the 75/25 mix, the alternative markets or the capped-beta option; 'outperformed by a long way' is unquantified.

Judes says Winton lowered volatility ahead of the 2013 taper tantrum due to a correlation scenario, which is a discretionary-looking risk call alongside a claim that trend should not be timed or regime-switched; the boundary between risk overlay and timing is not defined.

Statement that Winton has not changed its view since Harding's 2018 comment coexists with the observation that trend Sharpe has declined steadily since the 1970s; the product split is presented as a response, not a contradiction.

Alternative-market outperformance and barriers to entry are given as the reasons for extra return, but the same crowding logic that explains trend's decline would predict erosion as more managers extend into these markets; not addressed.

The replication fee (about 95bp) is the host's figure, and Judes says he has not looked closely at replication products, so his rejection of the single-manager-risk claim rests on logic rather than study.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Judes names few price-leading inputs: the stock-bond correlation (modestly positive due to inflation) and the direction of news (disinflationary and negative for growth) as the key scenario for a short-bond, long-equity trend book; central bank intervention timing is treated as unforecastable by systematic managers. Longer-term he treats the number of traders in trend following as the driver of expected trend Sharpe, with 0.5 as the planning figure, and the effective number of independent markets as the driver of diversification benefit. Horizons are scenario-based (days to weeks for stress tests) and multi-year for Sharpe.
reader_inferences: (reader) Winton's stance is built around process: scientific research controls, human responsibility for key parameters, a fixed product mix and scenario risk management, with the investor experience (drawdowns, committees) as an explicit design input.
(reader) The 75/25 mix, the alternative-market expansion and the product split can be read as three responses to the same belief that stand-alone trend Sharpe is about 0.5 and falling.

(reader) Judes separates what is knowable (long-run markets trend; crowding lowers Sharpe) from what is not (timing of trend, Fed behaviour), and builds rules around the second category by refusing to act on it.
(reader) Kaastrup-Larsen's portfolio-Sharpe framing and Judes's investor-experience framing converge on the argument against evaluating trend on stand-alone Sharpe or crisis labels.

added_claims.speaker: Simon Judes
added_claims.quote: this apparently technical statistical decision about which is the best speed at that moment amounts to just a call on what the FED is going to do and when
added_claims.claim: Choosing a faster trend speed mid-selloff looks technical but is actually a bet on when the Fed will step in: right if intervention comes later, wrong if it comes at once, roughly neutral if it never comes.
added_claims.indicator: trend speed switch conditional on regime
added_claims.conditions: market falling for about two weeks while long equities
added_claims.testable: partly - could be tested with regime-conditional speed rules, but argument is scenario logic

added_claims.speaker: Simon Judes
added_claims.quote: by definition anything that has happened is realistic because it did happen
added_claims.claim: Stress scenarios drawn from history are realistic by definition, whereas 'the worst that could happen' (everything to zero) is not helpful; so Winton replays current positions through past environments.
added_claims.indicator: worst historical day/week for current positions
added_claims.testable: yes - replay of positions through history

added_claims.speaker: Simon Judes
added_claims.quote: this idea that Trend following is a kind of dumb strategy that is just people following each other
added_claims.claim: The belief Winton most disagrees with about trend following is that it is a dumb herding strategy in which people follow each other.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: I don't really see a huge difference in long-term performance
added_claims.claim: Comparing managers that trade the 50-60 classical markets with those trading hundreds, the host sees different performance at different times but no huge difference in long-term performance.
